For those of us on the outside, what we read is that, at least for asset creation—say I’m a game designer, I’m supposed to build this game quickly, but now I have to create all these trees and houses in the game—is that a place where AI is heavily used now?

Piero Molino. I would say these days, in the last year or so, that’s where many gaming studios are focusing.

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Piero Molino. With not a great response from at least one side of the public, in particular in the U.S. and other Western markets.

Ben Lorica. So the reason, Piero, is that they can tell it was created by AI?

Piero Molino. Yeah. On one hand, they can tell, but I also think it’s a more philosophical argument: these models have very often been trained on data from the internet without the consent of the original creators and things like that.

So it’s a combination of perceived lower quality plus the perceived—

Ben Lorica. Ethical issues. So is the perceived lower quality justified?

Piero Molino. I would say right now, yes, still—although that may not be the case soon enough.

I also think most companies will start to do something relatively smart. If there’s a character in the game and this is the main character of the game, you probably always want to have it drawn by hand by a human. But if it’s one of the hundreds of tree assets that you have in the background—

Ben Lorica. Yeah.

Piero Molino. —maybe that’s less important. I think developers will get smart about how they use these tools too.

Ben Lorica. All right. So edge versus cloud. That’s an important part of what you do, and you’ve already touched on cost as a main motivation.

First of all, before we go any further, in your case, the models you need are multimodal, right? They’re not just text. They need to be able to create images, sound, video. Is that correct?

Piero Molino. Yeah. Basically, that technological layer that we created, which we call the AI engine—similar to how people call them physics engines—can do many different things.

It can generate text. It can generate structured text. It can generate images and audio. It can take user input in text, images, and audio.

It’s basically a multimodal mechanism that also has additional capabilities like embeddings, search, semantic search, and classification.

Ben Lorica. What about CAD design, where you have these 3D assets? Do you need models that are able to do that?

Piero Molino. Right now, we don’t support the generation of 3D assets on the fly yet because that’s a little bit more involved and—

Ben Lorica. It seems like that’s a direction some of these world models are going—

Piero Molino. Yeah, the world models are going in a direction—

Ben Lorica. The ones that are targeting games.

Piero Molino. Yeah. There are many people doing many different things.

Some of them are pure frame-to-frame, image-to-video or video-to-video generation. Others are more like: I render something in a bare-bones 3D world, like a gray-box 3D world, and then I slap some style-transfer mechanism on top of it that changes the style of the game in real time.

There are many different people doing many different things there.

Ben Lorica. But the bottom line is that when you say “model,” you’re actually describing something beyond text generation.

Piero Molino. Yeah. It’s text, image, audio, all together.

Ben Lorica. And our listeners who interact with some of the frontier models like Gemini or ChatGPT know they can generate multimodal assets, but they are in the cloud.

So one of the things you’re trying to do is lower your costs by not using these expensive APIs.

Piero Molino. Yeah, exactly.

Ben Lorica. And secondly, to run on device, where “device,” broadly speaking, could be a laptop, mobile phone, and so on and so forth.

Which means, what is your base model? Is it one of the open-weights Chinese models?

Piero Molino. Basically, for each of the tasks, we have separate models. They’re kind of like building blocks.

Ben Lorica. Is it something Studio Atelico created from scratch, or did you take one of the open-weights models and start from there?

Piero Molino. It depends on the specific component. In some cases, we are building our own models. In other cases, they are open models that we are adapting, compressing—

Ben Lorica. Building your own model means data—

Piero Molino. Right.

Ben Lorica. Getting the data and then the compute. So what you’re saying is that this is doable for you?

Piero Molino. Yeah. For large models—say, 100 billion parameters plus—that requires a lot of data and a lot of compute.

Ben Lorica. That’s a lab.

Piero Molino. The nice thing for us is that the models we run are in the millions of parameters or very small billions—like one billion or three billion at most.

Ben Lorica. And the reason, Piero, is that ultimately you want to be able to run it on device.

Piero Molino. Exactly. The fact that we use these smaller models makes it so that training them from scratch is not as expensive as training 100-billion-parameter models.

Ben Lorica. And the data for pretraining is just public data?

Piero Molino. Exactly. For instance, if you look at models from both Hugging Face and NVIDIA—and now Hugging Face plus NVIDIA—for text, they’re all using data where the recipes are shared, if you want.

Ben Lorica. You mean the data recipe? Is this the Nemotron family?

Piero Molino. Yeah, exactly, the Nemotron family. They have the recipe for training and the data they’ve been using all available.

Ben Lorica. But your models are multimodal.

Piero Molino. Yeah. We actually have different models for each modality, and then we put them together in different ways.

For some modalities, like speech, for instance, you can get away with smaller models. We want to be on the Pareto frontier of how big the model is—meaning how small a footprint it can have in RAM on a device—versus how fast it can generate things, versus how high quality it is.

Ben Lorica. Throughput and latency.

Piero Molino. Throughput, latency, and quality. Because you can get something very, very fast, but if it’s not good enough, it’s not usable. But if you have something super high quality that is super slow or requires more RAM than the device has, that’s also not useful.

So you want to be at the intersection of all of these.

Ben Lorica. And there are models that you use to develop your own games, and then there are models that have to run on device as people are playing the games.

Piero Molino. Exactly. For building our own games, we use coding assistants and things like that, so it’s not like we’re doing anything substantially different from anybody else.

But for what we run on device, it’s a combination of some open source models that we fine-tune for the specific game—because those models are small enough that they’re also cheap to fine-tune—and some of our own models.

If you don’t fine-tune them, they’re usually not high quality enough for running the game.

For instance, for speech, we have our own text-to-speech model that is on the order of 100 million parameters. So it’s not that large, but it’s high quality enough to sound good to the players and can also run on device. It’s a good intersection.

Ben Lorica. And so when you run the models on device, on a phone or a laptop, how does that impact someone’s battery life?

Piero Molino. Right.

Ben Lorica. And is the inference always being done on GPUs or CPUs?

Piero Molino. It depends on the different devices.

For instance, on iOS devices like the iPhone—our first game, Bobium Brawlers, will release first on iOS—Apple has, first of all, very good hardware, but also a layer that is not exactly like CUDA but is similar in spirit. It’s called Metal.

With Metal, you can write kernels against it, and it decides where to run your computation—on the GPU, NPU, or CPU.

Ben Lorica. And you can use coding agents to write your kernels.

Piero Molino. Right. Yeah, we also use them for that, for sure. But writing kernels is a little bit of an art, right?

Ben Lorica. Oh yeah. You need people who have actually done it.

Piero Molino. Exactly. I’m fortunate enough to have spent some time in the Hazy Research Lab at Stanford, where FlashAttention comes from and things like that.

I was exposed to these kinds of things very early on, and that keeps helping me these days to write very efficient kernels that otherwise would not have been as easy to write, even with the use of coding agents.

We have a little bit of secret sauce there. I won’t get into the details of it, but you can imagine it as a compiler—a kernel compiler—that makes it so we have very, very efficient kernels.

Ben Lorica. So then you have a pipeline for customizing models, or post-training them—whatever that means: fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, whatever it takes to make them better.

Piero Molino. You already mentioned it, actually. We are using more or less Ludwig for doing that.

Ben Lorica. Yeah. You’ve developed a pipeline for doing this, but to some extent the pipeline depends on how good the base models are. And you’ve described the base models as a mixture of things you’ve pretrained from scratch and a bunch of open-weights models that you can then customize or post-train.

So generally speaking, Piero, if you were describing this to people who haven’t gone that far down the road of post-training or customizing models—especially the ones they want to run locally—

Piero Molino. Right.

Ben Lorica. I’ve heard Pete Warden describe these local models as actually not being that far behind the frontier models, depending on the task. You know Pete Warden?

Piero Molino. Yeah.

Ben Lorica. So we’re not talking years; we’re talking months. Do you agree with that assessment?

Piero Molino. Yeah. I have a couple of pointers that could be interesting for the listeners.

On one hand, if you go to Apple AI, they do a bunch of analysis and comparisons. They have some results that are actually from last year, but they apply this year too. Fundamentally, they were showing that, depending on the task, open models that you can run on devices lag behind by maybe six months on some tasks and nine to 10 months on others compared with—

Ben Lorica. Without customization and fine-tuning.

Piero Molino. That’s without customization, exactly. So already, the lag isn’t that large. And you can fill that gap by doing customization, post-training, fine-tuning of sorts.

There’s another example that’s a little older. I think it’s from the beginning of 2024. When I was at Predibase, we released this paper called LoriLand, where we trained 1,200 fine-tuned models on 30 different tasks, each of them using different base models.

Some of the base models were one-billion-parameter models, some were eight-billion-parameter models, and there was everything in between.

After fine-tuning on the specific task, they were reaching the same level of quality as what were the best models at the time—GPT-4, basically—at a fraction of the cost.

The vast majority of the value was coming from the data for the task. The base model was more or less an independent variable. The actual effect was coming from the fine-tuning and the increased performance that you get after post-training.

Ben Lorica. So in many ways, these small specialized models are what make your architecture possible.

Piero Molino. Yes.

Ben Lorica. The question is, if I’m a game developer or game designer, how easy is it for me to replicate what you’ve done?

In other words, does every game studio need to do what you do, unless of course they work with you? How easy is it for a game studio to develop the assets that you have?

Piero Molino. There are two aspects to it.

One is the inference side—not the training or post-training part, but inference. On inference, I would say we’ve solved, or are solving, those kinds of problems for other people too.

At some point—we haven’t announced it yet—we want to release the engine in a way that other people can license it and use it.

Ben Lorica. So you’ll be like Unity.

Piero Molino. Not like Unity, because it’s not a game engine. It’s just an AI engine. So it’s just the AI side.

I would say the most similar thing is Havok, which makes a physics engine. It integrates with Unity, Unreal, Godot, but it’s not the entire game engine. It’s just that specific component.

On the other hand, to make the game work really well—in particular with the LLM side of things, but also with the other aspects like image generation and audio generation—and also to govern it and get it to do what you want, there is this process of post-training.

We are trying to make that process as easy as possible for ourselves. Again, my experience with Ludwig is what I’m bringing from my previous company and my previous open source contributions.

In that case, it’s just a configuration file. You don’t have to know all the details of how to implement the post-training, how to collect the data, and all of that.

There’s also a little data collector that you can put in front and after. You can wrap a classic OpenAI call with that thing, and it collects inputs and outputs. Then you can use those for doing the post-training.

You can run the game with large models, collect inputs and outputs, and then fine-tune a small model on those inputs and outputs to mimic the larger model.

It’s still more involved, but it’s not extremely complicated. With the help of someone like us, I think for gaming companies it’s going to become easier and easier to do this kind of adaptation.

Another reason for doing it is not just quality, but also control.

For instance, in our game, Bobium Brawlers, we have image generation, and we’re doing post-training of the image-generation models not because the base models aren’t good enough, but because we want the output to follow the style of our own artists.

The best way to do that is to have your artist draw what you want and then train on that. At runtime, when a user or player asks for a specific creature, they get an image of that creature that represents what they asked for, but the thickness of the lines, the style of the colors—everything about the art style in general—reflects the style of our own internal artists.

So that’s very important. It’s not just a matter of quality; it’s also a matter of control.

Ben Lorica. Because you rely on the device for inference, in many ways the device becomes your cloud—your deployment boundary.

In the cloud, I’m only as good as the GPUs in the cloud provider. In your case, if my iPhone isn’t good enough, then it won’t work. So the device becomes your deployment boundary in some ways.

That’s why I think you have a minimum version of the iPhone that you support, right?

Piero Molino. Yeah. For this game, we’re basically targeting an iPhone 12 Pro and an iPhone 14.

In the engine, though, for each modality we support many different models of different sizes and, obviously, different quality.

You can imagine, from both a developer perspective and potentially a user perspective in the future, that there could be a slider—like the resolution slider in a video game for visual quality—except there could be a slider for intelligence, if you want.

If I’m on weaker hardware, I can only run so large a model. If I’m on stronger hardware, I can run a larger model. So I can interpolate between those things in the future.

Additionally, I would say we have tailwinds on the hardware side because a pretty consistent observation throughout the years of hardware innovation is that whatever is today the best workstation hardware, costing $5,000 to $10,000, will in a couple of years be your average laptop, more or less.

You can already see it with hardware like the NVIDIA DGX Spark, the new laptops, AMD Halo, and the Mac Studio.

The direction everybody is going in is unified memory combined with strong inference hardware. The DGX, for instance, has 128 gigabytes of unified memory. If you have that much unified memory, it becomes relatively easier to run a model that is large enough to be pretty capable.

Today, the DGX Spark costs whatever—$5,000. Two years from now, that’s going to be what everybody has in their pockets.

Ben Lorica. Yeah. You raise an important point. A lot of articles are written about GPUs and GPU shortages, but actually the bottlenecks are electricity and memory.

Have you been following high-bandwidth flash?

Piero Molino. Oh, this one I’m not familiar with.

Ben Lorica. It’s interesting because there might be some things you can offload to high-bandwidth flash in the future. Obviously, right now it’s a bit early.

Piero Molino. Flash meaning nonvolatile flash?

Ben Lorica. Yeah, similar to what SSDs did—

Piero Molino. Got it.

Ben Lorica. —but for memory. It’s early, but I think people are excited about it.

Your focus is on mobile phones, right? What about games for laptops? Obviously, the same technology would apply there. Is anyone doing something similar to what you’re doing for games on laptops?

Piero Molino. Not that I’m aware of, honestly.

For us, doing a mobile game first was a little bit like fighting the final boss. Because if you can make it run on an iPhone 13, obviously it runs much better on laptops and desktops.

Ben Lorica. And by the way, it’s not one-shot either, because every time they ship an update to the OS, they can update the model.

But I think recently Godot has gained steam and a following because of the changes Unity tried to implement at one point.

Ben Lorica. So Godot is like the open source Unity.

Piero Molino. I would say, yeah, more or less. Not exactly, but it’s the open source alternative to it.

Ben Lorica. So what are we talking about in terms of parity? Is it like Solaris versus Linux in the year 2000, where Solaris is still clearly better than Linux?

Piero Molino. Yeah, I would say probably right now that’s where we are.

And I wouldn’t say clearly better in absolute terms of quality or the quality of the games. I’m talking more in terms of adoption.

Ben Lorica. But if you look three or four years ahead, does the arc of history favor Godot because people will gravitate toward open source? Is that a fair prediction?

Piero Molino. I would say I hope so, honestly. I hope so because it feels like a better open alternative.

It’s already really good, but an even better open alternative—

Ben Lorica. What is the funding mechanism for Godot? Is there a foundation?

Piero Molino. There’s a foundation, and I think there are a bunch of companies that have spawned around it, created mostly by the maintainers to do services.

Ben Lorica. So it seems there might be a way to sustain the development.

Piero Molino. Yeah. Now it seems pretty self-sustaining, and I think in the past they received some grants from Microsoft and others.

Ben Lorica. Because Godot is open source and gaining popularity, you’re saying that there might be some pressure for different components of the game-development stack to become open source as well.

Piero Molino. That is definitely possible, yes.

Or, on the other hand, the closed source ones need to become substantially better so that their value is much more understood and much more worth it for developers when they’re making a decision.

Ben Lorica. Or what could happen is you folks could be the AI engine for Godot. Then, as it becomes popular, game developers will go, “Well, wait a minute. Why don’t we create an open source version of Atelico, since that’s an important part of the stack?”

But I don’t think, in the beginning at least, people will care, because they just want to create games.

Piero Molino. Exactly. I think it’s a matter of capabilities, really, more than anything else.

Also, making a game usually takes a long time. The cycles of adoption of any gaming technology are usually longer because, in particular, very large games take five or six years to make.

The decisions you make now, you’re going to stick with for six years.

Because of that slowness, let’s assume I’ve been building a game in Unity for the last four years and now a better engine comes out. I’m going to finish my game in Unity. Maybe for the next game I’ll consider an alternative.

The cost of switching would be very, very high.

Ben Lorica. What if Tencent releases an open source AI engine like Atelico? Is that plausible? I don’t want to make you nervous, but—

Piero Molino. No. That’s always the case, right? With every single thing you do as a company, there’s always, “What if Google does it? What if the incumbent does it?” and whatever else.

Ben Lorica. Well, in this case, Tencent is also heavily invested in games.

Piero Molino. Exactly. But Tencent also owns—I don’t remember exactly what share—part of Epic Games, which makes Unreal Engine.

There are many things happening in parallel.

For any startup, I think the advantage is, first of all, how fast you can move and how focused you are.

Tencent is a behemoth of—I don’t even know how many people, probably hundreds of thousands—versus us. We are seven people, and we are focused only on this. They do a million different things.

I think for every startup, at any stage, the focus and smallness of the team become assets that let you move fast, try different things, react very quickly, and be trailblazers.

It’s almost always the case that small companies are trailblazers, and then the other ones follow later. If the small company is successful, that’s always true for every startup.

Ben Lorica. All right. Let’s get you out of here with two quick questions.

The first one is coding and coding agents. How much do you rely on them, and what’s your take on the future of coding?

Piero Molino. Personally, and as a company, we rely on them. They’re a big part of our tooling.

At the same time, what I’ve discovered over the last year or so, since we’ve been using them more heavily, is that the exact same tool in the hands of different developers ends up producing quite different output.

I think the quality and experience of the individuals using the tools influence the results a lot.

For us, it’s not going to be a mechanism to cut costs of any sort. It’s more a mechanism to be faster. With the same number of people, you can be faster, as opposed to cutting people.

Ben Lorica. That statement you just made—in the hands of people who are good—but in the future, Piero, how do we know who’s good if everyone is using the same coding agents?

I just talked about this with someone. In math, which is where I came from, they now have a situation where generating a proof is easy. Maybe even writing the paper is easy because you can ask the AI to write the paper.

Now, whether or not the paper can be understood by mathematicians is a different thing.

Mathematicians are proposing that not only is generating the proof cheap, and maybe writing the paper is also cheap, but in order for a paper to be accepted, one, it has to be understood by humans who will accept it, and secondly, they’re discussing an additional requirement.

They might say, “Hey, Piero, you submitted this paper. We want you to give a talk about this paper in front of mathematicians.”

In terms of coding, I guess the equivalent would be some sort of code review. That’s how you discover, “Hey, this guy is the next Jeff Dean.”

Piero Molino. Yeah, that’s a great point. And I would say the role and decisions of—I think it’s like a—

Ben Lorica. By the way, for coding and math, you have generation, but the verification step is also doable because you have compilers and formal verifiers. You can even have the AI do the tests.

In other words, generate tests, verify, write the paper—or in the case of coding, generate the documentation. Everyone is on the same footing.

So what distinguishes the star from the non-star?

Piero Molino. Yeah. I think first of all it’s the “what.”

Ben Lorica. Okay.

Piero Molino. You have all the intelligence, quote-unquote, in what to work—

Ben Lorica. On. What to work on.

Piero Molino. What to work on. It’s a very important choice. It becomes the most important skill.

Ben Lorica. That’s still what remains in math, unless the AI solves all of the famous problems. But then after that, what?

Piero Molino. Yeah. Again, I think we’ll figure out that there are more problems.

At the limit, there’s always an infinite number of problems one could be solving.

Maybe it’s different between math and code, but—

Ben Lorica. In math, it’s a non-renewable resource. There are only so many interesting problems.

Piero Molino. At the same time, once you learn something—I’m sure this is always true in science—then you think about the consequences of what you’ve learned.

Ben Lorica. This is the case when the human does it, because the human will try to solve something, get stuck, go this way, explore, do a bunch of things, and then maybe say, “Oh, there are interesting problems here too.”

It’s not clear that the AI will do that.

Piero Molino. Right. You can have an outer loop that is kind of self-improving, but—

Ben Lorica. The human, in the course of exploring, has taste.

Piero Molino. Yeah. And whenever you learn something, that changes your mental model about the world and about—

Ben Lorica. Whereas the AI is just an optimization engine that’s trying to crunch through so much compute to give you the answer.

Piero Molino. Yeah. But you’re directing it somehow, right?

Even if you’re not directing it, you’re still creating the scaffolding that makes it so that it discovers a direction.

Ben Lorica. So there’s still the “what.” What do you think about this whole notion that you should be able to explain to me what—

Piero Molino. For scientific discoveries, definitely that is valuable because I think discovery without understanding—we couldn’t falsify it.

Ben Lorica. It would be like Einstein saying, “I have the theory of relativity, but I cannot give a talk about it.”

Piero Molino. Exactly. It’s not true knowledge if it’s not disseminated, and if we’re not able to disseminate it.

I think it’s similar in a sense for coding. You, as the developer, are the first critic of this thing. The critique is super valuable.

To give an example, let’s assume I’m creating a piece of code that needs to run on a device. Once it has been built, I try to run it on another device, and it breaks.

Maybe I didn’t make it clear from the very beginning which devices I wanted it to run on. But after the fact, I can critique it and say, “Well, this works here, but it doesn’t work there. That’s the new task you have to do. Now you have to make it work there.”

A human can also look at the generalization.

My personal experience has been that these models are extremely good at writing code, and sometimes even redundant code, and sometimes making patches on top of patches on top of patches.

In particular, because it’s so easy for them to write yet another piece of code, generalizing across multiple instances, multiple devices, or multiple different implementations of the same thing using design patterns is not always the first way they implement things or think about them.

There’s an argument to be made that it doesn’t matter—they can create yet another bespoke function. But their memory and context are also limited.

So if you create, let’s say, 100 different implementations of the same function for 100 different devices, they themselves, when something breaks, will not know where to look.

I think good software design principles are something a human can provide and influence the model toward.

Ben Lorica. Which, unfortunately, is somewhat gained through experience. But if you’re not gaining experience—

Piero Molino. Exactly. And that’s a problem.

If you are only using models from the very beginning, you don’t have the opportunity to gain that experience. That is a problem.

I think maybe that’s something to be said for schools, actually. Like, why would—

Ben Lorica. They need to rethink what they do and teach, right?

All right. Last question to get you out of here. Obviously, because of what you do, you need to pay attention to frontier models. We talked about world models, multimodal models.

Is there anything that excites you that you feel is somewhat below the radar that, in six months, more of us will be talking about?

Piero Molino. Interesting.

Obviously, I’m very excited about smaller models and things that run on the device and that whole space. I think some people are starting to pay more attention to it.

Ben Lorica. A lot more are beginning to, right?

Piero Molino. Exactly. I think there will be more of that. I’m preaching to the choir here, I’m sure, but it’s also the kind of thing I’m working on, so I’m excited about it.

Of the things I’m not directly working on, I think there’s an interesting space opening up around world models.

Specifically, I’m not a strong believer in, let’s say, the original formulation of world models as just: past frames plus controls equals next frame.

Fundamentally, I’m not convinced by that because the inductive bias has so little structure that you would require an incredible amount of data to make it do anything reasonable.

And then when there’s a bug, you don’t know what to do. If it does something different, what are you going to do? You’re going to create much, much more data to try to compensate for errors.

I think it’s a recipe for not-great outcomes.

But what I’m seeing is the beginning of people starting to inject some structure. So you get a blending of structures that come from game engines together with some of the techniques of world models and style transfer, et cetera.

The blending of these two things, I think, is interesting and promising.

Maybe not exactly for video games as we understand them today, but for potentially creating new kinds of interactive experiences that we haven’t thought about up until now.

That could be interesting—more interactive-movie-style things rather than, strictly speaking, games. I’m interested in that. I think it could be fun.

Ben Lorica. And with that, thank you, Piero. Always great to catch up with you.

Piero Molino. Likewise, Ben. Thanks for having me. It was a pleasure chatting with you again.
